mainTopic: מכת מדינה in a farm rental: when a tenant may subtract from his rent, how luck and merit affect the claim, and related rules about counting years
overview: The משנה taught that a tenant whose rented field was struck by blight may subtract from his rent only if it was a מכת מדינה, a disaster that hit most of the valley. The גמרא first asks 'what if' questions about different crops and different kinds of blight, and these stay unresolved (תיקו). It then rules that a tenant who planted barley instead of the wheat he was told to plant cannot subtract. It also rules that the owner's bad luck does not count as a regional disaster, because bad luck always leaves a little. And if all of the tenant's own fields were struck, the owner can blame the tenant's bad luck. Next, the גמרא raises an objection from a משנה in ערכין about years of blight. רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that a sold field follows a special פסוק about 'years of crops,' and this leads to a back-and-forth about שביעית. Finally, שמואל rules that a tenant who never planted cannot subtract, since the owner's merit might have saved the field. רב ששת challenges this from a shepherd who left his flock, and that discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Questions about different crops and different kinds of damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes one question and adds more: does it count as a regional disaster if the surrounding fields had a different crop, or a different kind of damage?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the law? If the other fields had a different seed, what is the law? Is wheat compared to barley considered a different seed or not? If the whole world was struck by windblast and his field by mildew, or the whole world by mildew and his field by windblast, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a string of 'what if' questions about whether a disaster still counts as a מכת מדינה when the tenant's field does not exactly match the rest of the valley.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule so far is that the tenant may subtract only if most of the valley was struck. These questions test what 'the same disaster' means. If the neighbors grew a different crop, or were hit by a different kind of blight, maybe his loss is not truly part of the regional disaster.

keyTerms.meaning: a different type of seed or crop
windblast: crops dried out and blackened by a hot wind
mildew: crops turning pale and yellow

phrases.english: What is the law? A different seed, what is the law?
Wheat in relation to barley,
phrases.notes: Some versions say שעורים, the Hebrew word; the corrected wording in square brackets says שערי, the Aramaic word. Both mean barley.

phrases.english: is it considered like a different seed, or not?
The entire world was struck by windblast,
phrases.notes: 'The entire world' here means all the surrounding fields.

phrases.english: and his field by mildew,

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי: כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ בְּיֵרָקוֹן,
phrases.english: or alternatively: the entire world was struck by mildew,
and his field by windblast, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of questions defining מכת מדינה from before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a disaster count as regional when the tenant's crop or type of damage differs from the rest of the valley?

steps.title: The questions stay unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finds no answer, so the questions are left standing: תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says תיקו: there is no proof either way, so these questions stay open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו does not mean the question was silly. It means the גמרא could not find a source that decides it, so the doubt remains.

keyTerms.meaning: 'let it stand': the question remains unresolved

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the questions of step 1 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: No ruling is reached on different crops or different kinds of blight.

steps.title: The tenant planted barley instead of the wheat he was told to plant
steps.stepSummary: The owner said to plant wheat, the tenant planted barley, and both most of the valley and his barley were blasted. May he subtract from the rent?
steps.simpleTranslation: The owner told him: plant it with wheat. He went and planted barley. Most of the valley was blasted, and his barley was blasted too. What is the law? Can the tenant say: even if I had planted wheat it would have been blasted too? Or can the owner say: had you planted wheat, the פסוק 'you shall decree a matter and it will be established for you' would have come true for me?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question: does a regional disaster still help the tenant when he broke the deal and planted a different crop?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tenant argues that the whole valley was struck, so wheat would have failed too. The owner argues that if his wishes had been followed, he might have been blessed and his crop spared, as the פסוק promises that what a person decrees comes true. So the question is whether the tenant's change of crop takes away his right to subtract.

keyTerms.meaning: he can say to him (he has a valid claim)

phrases.english: He said to him: Plant it with wheat,
phrases.notes: The owner of the field is speaking to his tenant.

phrases.english: and he went and planted it with barley,
and most of the valley was blasted,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִשְׁתְּדוּף נָמֵי הָנָךְ שְׂעָרֵי דִּילֵיהּ, מַאי?
phrases.english: and these barley crops of his were also blasted, what is the law?
Do we say that he can say to him:

phrases.aramaic: אִילּוּ זְרַעְתַּהּ חִיטֵּי הֲוָה נָמֵי מִשְׁתַּדְפָא,
phrases.english: Had I planted it with wheat, it would also have been blasted,
or perhaps he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Now it is the owner talking.

phrases.english: Had you planted it with wheat,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה מִקַּיַּים בִּי ״וְתִגְזַר אֹמֶר וְיָקׇם לָךְ״?
phrases.english: there would have been fulfilled in me: 'And you shall decree a matter and it will be established for you'?
phrases.notes: איוב 22:28

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: זִרְעַהּ חִיטֵּי, וַאֲזַל הוּא וְזַרְעַהּ שְׂעָרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the תיקו, a new question about a tenant who changed the crop.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can a tenant who planted a different crop than agreed still subtract for a regional disaster?

steps.title: The owner's argument wins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא decides that the owner can say: had you planted wheat, the blessing of the פסוק would have come true for me.
steps.simpleTranslation: It stands to reason that he can say to him: had you planted wheat, there would have been fulfilled in me 'And you shall decree a matter and it will be established for you, and light shall shine on your ways.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of step 3 in the owner's favor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the tenant did not follow the owner's instructions, he cannot claim that wheat would have failed too. The owner may have merited a blessing if his decision had been carried out, so the tenant cannot subtract from the rent.

keyTerms.meaning: it stands to reason; it makes sense
'you shall decree a matter and it will be established for you' (איוב)

steps.whatToRemember: A tenant who planted a different crop than the owner told him cannot use a regional disaster to lower his rent, because the owner can say his own choice might have been blessed.

phrases.english: It stands to reason that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' here is the owner.

phrases.english: Had you planted it with wheat,
there would have been fulfilled in me:
'And you shall decree a matter and it will be established for you,
and light shall shine upon your ways.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner's claim is accepted; the tenant who changed the crop cannot subtract.

steps.title: All the owner's fields were blasted, but most of the valley was not
steps.stepSummary: If all the owner's fields, including this one, were blasted but most of the valley was fine, may the tenant subtract because of the owner's bad luck?
steps.simpleTranslation: All the fields of the owner were blasted, and this one was blasted with them, but most of the valley was not blasted. What is the law? Do we say that since most of the valley was not blasted, he does not subtract for him? Or perhaps, since all of the owner's lands were blasted, the tenant can say to him: this happened because of your bad luck, for all your fields were blasted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question: can the owner's personal bad luck count like a regional disaster?
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the normal rule, the tenant cannot subtract, because most of the valley was fine. But here every field the owner owns was struck, which points to the owner's own bad fortune rather than the tenant's. The question is whether that is enough to let the tenant subtract.

keyTerms.meaning: the owner who rents out his field

phrases.english: All the fields of the owner were blasted,
and this one was also blasted with them,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the field the tenant is renting.

phrases.english: but most of the valley was not blasted, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן כֵּיוָן דְּלָא אִשְׁתְּדוּף רוּבָּא דְבָאגָא
phrases.english: Do we say: since most of the valley was not blasted,
he does not subtract for him,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאִשְׁתְּדוּף כּוּלְּהוּ אַרְעָתֵיהּ,
phrases.english: or perhaps, since all his lands were blasted,
he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The tenant is the one speaking to the owner.

phrases.english: This is because of your own bad luck,
for all your fields were blasted.
phrases.notes: Some versions say משתדפו; the corrected wording in square brackets says נשתדפו. The meaning is the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question, the reverse of the usual rule: the owner's fields were struck, but the region was not.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the owner's personal bad luck (all his fields struck) let the tenant subtract, even without a regional disaster?

steps.title: Bad luck always leaves a little behind
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers Step 5. The owner can say his own bad luck could not have caused this, because bad luck still leaves a little, as the פסוק in ירמיהו says.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that the owner can say: If this had happened because of my bad luck, a little would have been left for me, as it is written: 'For we are left a few out of many.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about the owner's bad luck. The owner can say his bad luck is not the cause, since his field was wiped out completely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner proves from a פסוק that someone with bad luck still keeps a little ('a few out of many'). Since this field was wiped out completely, the owner's bad luck is not the cause. Most of the valley was not struck, so it is not a מכת מדינה either, and the tenant may not subtract from the rent.

keyTerms.meaning: It stands to reason, it makes sense
As it is written (a פסוק is coming)

phrases.english: It stands to reason that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Here the owner is speaking to the tenant.

phrases.english: If it were because of my bad luck,
a little would have been left for me,
as it is written: "For we are left a few out of many."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 42:2

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner's bad luck is not the cause, because bad luck leaves a little. Since most of the valley was not struck, there is no regional disaster, and the tenant does not subtract.

steps.title: All the tenant's fields were blasted too
steps.stepSummary: A new case: most of the valley was blasted, this field was blasted, and also every field the tenant owns was blasted. Does the regional disaster count, or is it the tenant's bad luck?
steps.simpleTranslation: If all of the tenant's own fields were blasted, and most of the valley was blasted, and this field was blasted with them, what is the law? Do we say that since most of the valley was blasted, the tenant subtracts from the rent? Or perhaps, since all of the tenant's lands were blasted, the owner can say: It is because of your bad luck, since all your fields were blasted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the mirror image of Step 5. This time it is the tenant whose own fields were all destroyed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two reasons pull in opposite directions. Most of the valley was hit, which sounds like a regional disaster that lets the tenant subtract. But every one of the tenant's own fields was hit too, so the owner can claim the tenant's personal bad luck caused it.

keyTerms.meaning: A tenant who pays a fixed amount of produce as rent
Was blasted (crops ruined by a hot wind)

phrases.english: All the tenant's own fields were blasted
and most of the valley was blasted,
and this field was also blasted with them, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן כֵּיוָן דְּאִשְׁתְּדוּף רוּבָּא דְבָאגָא
phrases.english: Do we say: since most of the valley was blasted
he subtracts from the owner's rent,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאִשְׁתְּדוּף כּוּלְּהוּ אַרְעָתֵיהּ,
phrases.english: or perhaps, since all his lands were blasted,
the owner can say to him:
It is because of your bad luck,
for all your fields were blasted.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean "were blasted."

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמְרִינַן כֵּיוָן דְּאִשְׁתְּדוּף רוּבָּא דְבָאגָא מְנַכֵּי לֵיהּ, אוֹ דִלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips the case of Step 5: now the tenant's fields, not the owner's, were all blasted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When all the tenant's fields were blasted along with most of the valley, can the tenant still subtract, or can the owner blame the tenant's bad luck?

steps.title: The owner can blame the tenant's bad luck
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא decides that the owner can say the loss came from the tenant's bad luck, so the tenant may not subtract.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that the owner can say to him: It is because of your bad luck.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 7. The owner wins: the loss is blamed on the tenant's own bad luck.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since every field the tenant has was destroyed, the bad luck clearly follows the tenant. So the tenant pays the full rent even though most of the valley was also hit.

keyTerms.meaning: That he can say to him

phrases.english: It stands to reason that he can say to him:
It is because of your bad luck.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִסְתַּבְּרָא דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: מִשּׁוּם לַתָּאךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner can blame the tenant's bad luck, so the tenant does not subtract.

steps.title: Why can't the tenant use the same פסוק?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges Step 8: the tenant should be able to make the same argument the owner made in Step 6, that bad luck always leaves a little.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Here too, let the tenant say to the owner: If it were because of my bad luck, a little would have been left for me, since the פסוק 'For we are left a few out of many' would have come true for me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ruling of Step 8 is right. It uses the owner's own argument from Step 6 against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 6, total destruction proved it was not the owner's bad luck. The same logic should work for the tenant: his fields were totally destroyed, so it cannot be his bad luck either. This seems to contradict Step 8.

phrases.english: Why? Here too, let him say to him:
phrases.notes: Now it is the tenant speaking to the owner.

phrases.english: If it were because of my bad luck,
a little would have been left for me,
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are added by the corrected wording.

phrases.english: since this would have come true for me:
"For we are left a few out of many."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of Step 8 using the reasoning of Step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in Step 8 that the owner can blame the tenant's bad luck.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'bad luck leaves a little' argument that helped the owner in Step 6 should help the tenant just as well.

steps.title: The little would have been left in the tenant's own fields
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the owner can say that if the tenant deserved to have something left, it would have been left in the tenant's own fields, not in the owner's field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the owner can say to him: If you were worthy of having something left for you, it would have been left for you from your own fields.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of Step 9. The tenant's argument does not work against the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'little left over' from bad luck does not have to be in the rented field. If the tenant deserved anything, it should have shown up in his own land. Since nothing was left there either, the tenant's bad luck is fully to blame, and Step 8 stands.
steps.whatToRemember: When most of the valley is blasted, the tenant subtracts from the rent. But if all of the tenant's own fields were also blasted, the owner can blame the tenant's bad luck, and the tenant pays in full.

phrases.english: Because the owner can say to him:

phrases.aramaic: אִי הֲוָה חֲזֵית לְאִישְׁתַּיּוֹרֵי לָךְ מִידֵּי –
phrases.english: If you were worthy of having something left for you,
it would have been left for you from your own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9 and keeps the ruling of Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the leftover would appear in the unlucky person's own property, not in someone else's.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The tenant could use the 'bad luck leaves a little' argument just like the owner did.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tenant's leftover should have been in his own fields; since nothing remained there, the bad luck is his.

steps.title: An objection from the משנה about years of blasted crops
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins an objection from a משנה in ערכין: years of blasting, mildew, שביעית, or drought like in the days of אליהו do not count toward the number of years.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: If it was a year of blasting and mildew, or a שביעית year, or the years were like the years of אליהו, it does not count for him toward the number of years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up an objection against the rule that a tenant subtracts in a regional disaster. Here it only quotes the משנה; the actual point of the challenge comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a year of blasted crops does not count toward the waiting years of someone who sold his field. The גמרא will soon use this to question how regional disasters are treated in our case.

keyTerms.meaning: Crops blasted by a hot wind
The seventh year, when fields are not worked

phrases.english: They raised an objection: If it was a year of blasting and mildew,
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in ערכין 29b about someone who sold his field and must wait two years before buying it back.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שְׁבִיעִית, אוֹ שֶׁהָיוּ שָׁנִים כִּשְׁנֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ –
phrases.english: or the seventh year, or the years were like the years of Eliyahu,
phrases.notes: The years with no rain in מלכים א 17:1.

phrases.english: it does not count for him toward the number.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge from a משנה, aimed at the basic rule that a regional disaster lets the tenant subtract.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a tenant subtracts from the rent when there is a regional disaster.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only: the משנה about years of blasted crops not counting is quoted here; the גמרא will draw the contradiction in the next step.

steps.title: The inference from the משנה: some produce means the year counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the challenge. The משנה groups blasting and mildew with the drought of אליהו, when nothing grew at all. So if some produce did grow, the year counts, and it is not called a מכת מדינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה teaches blasting and mildew alongside 'years like the years of אליהו.' In אליהו's years there was no produce at all, so blasting and mildew must also mean no produce at all. But if there was some produce, the year counts for him, and we do not say it was a regional disaster!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from the משנה in ערכין that it started quoting in Step 11. That inference seems to contradict the earlier idea that partial blight is a regional disaster.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because blasting is listed next to אליהו's total drought, it must mean total failure. That implies a year with partial blight is treated as a normal year, not as a מכת מדינה. This clashes with the earlier ruling that blight over most of the valley counts as a regional disaster that lets the tenant subtract.

keyTerms.meaning: similar to, in the same category as
the years of drought in the time of אליהו, when nothing grew
it counts for him (toward the number of years)
a regional disaster, a blow to the whole area

phrases.english: It teaches: blasting and mildew
similar to years like the years of Elijah,

phrases.aramaic: מָה שְׁנֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ – דְּלָא הֲוַי תְּבוּאָה כְּלָל,
phrases.english: just as the years of Elijah were when there was no produce at all,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הָכָא נָמֵי – דְּלָא הֲוַי תְּבוּאָה כְּלָל.
phrases.english: so too here, it means when there was no produce at all.
But where there is some produce, it counts for him,
phrases.notes: It counts toward the years the buyer must hold the field before the seller can buy it back.

phrases.english: and we do not say it is a regional disaster!

steps.triggerLanguage: קָתָנֵי: שִׁדָּפוֹן וְיֵרָקוֹן דּוּמְיָא דְּשָׁנִים כִּשְׁנֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the objection that Step 11 started quoting
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that partial blight in most of the valley counts as a regional disaster
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה treats only total failure as a non-year. So partial failure counts as a normal year and is not a מכת מדינה.

steps.title: A sold field follows a special פסוק about years of produce
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that a sold field is different. The פסוק counts 'years of crops,' meaning years when there is produce anywhere in the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: There it is different, because the פסוק says, 'According to the number of years of crops he shall sell to you.' This means years in which there is produce in the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It says the rule for a sold field comes from a special פסוק, so it teaches nothing about tenants and regional disasters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a sold field, the תורה measures years by whether produce exists anywhere in the world. That is why only a total failure, like אליהו's drought, stops a year from counting. A tenant's case has no such פסוק, so partial blight there can still be a מכת מדינה.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
There it is different, because the verse says:
"According to the number of years of crops he shall sell to you,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:15

phrases.english: meaning years in which there is produce in the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: a special פסוק governs sold fields
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה in ערכין shows that partial blight is never a regional disaster.
steps.terutzMaskana: Sold fields follow a פסוק that counts any year with produce in the world, so the משנה does not apply to tenants.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer creates a new standard, 'produce in the world,' and the next two challenges test it.

steps.title: Then שביעית should count, since produce grows outside ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי challenges: if the measure is produce anywhere in the world, then שביעית should count toward the years, because produce grows outside ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to רב כהנא: If so, שביעית should count for him in the number of years, since there is produce outside ארץ ישראל!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the 'produce in the world' answer from Step 13. It points to a known rule: שביעית does not count toward the years of a sold field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed שביעית as a year that does not count. But in שביעית, produce does grow in the world, in חוץ לארץ. So by the new standard, שביעית should count.

keyTerms.meaning: if so, then according to that
it should count for him in the number of years

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to Rav Kahana:

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה שְׁבִיעִית תַּעֲלֶה לוֹ מִן הַמִּנְיָן,
phrases.english: If so, the Sabbatical Year should count for him in the number of years,
since there is produce outside the Land!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's standard of 'produce in the world'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The standard would make שביעית count, but the משנה says it does not.

steps.title: שביעית is cancelled by the King
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers that שביעית is a 'cancellation by the King.' The תורה itself removes that year, so it does not count no matter what grows elsewhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: שביעית is a cancellation by the King.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the 'produce in the world' standard by explaining why שביעית is a separate case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שביעית does not fail to count because of missing produce. It fails to count because ה׳, the King, takes the land out of the owner's use that year. So the 'produce in the world' test never applies to it.

keyTerms.meaning: a cancellation by the King, meaning a year taken away by ה׳'s decree

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שְׁבִיעִית אַפְקַעְתָּא דְמַלְכָּא הִיא.
phrases.english: He said to him: The Sabbatical Year is a cancellation by the King.
phrases.notes: The 'King' here is ה׳. In שביעית the land is taken out of the owner's use by His command.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different reason: שביעית is excluded by ה׳'s decree, not by a lack of produce
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שביעית should count because produce grows in חוץ לארץ.
steps.terutzMaskana: שביעית is removed by the King's decree, so it does not count.

steps.title: Then שביעית should not count for the yearly deduction either
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא challenges: if שביעית is cancelled, it should also not count when figuring the yearly price of redeeming a consecrated field. Yet the משנה charges a סלע and a פונדיון for every year.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא son of רב מרי said to רבינא: If so, שביעית should not count for him in the deduction! Why then did we learn: he gives a סלע and a פונדיון per year!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the 'cancelled by the King' answer from Step 15, using a different law that does count שביעית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When someone redeems a field he gave to הקדש, the price is set per year. The משנה charges a סלע and a פונדיון for every year, and that includes שביעית. If שביעית were truly cancelled, it should be left out of that count.

keyTerms.meaning: deduction, the per-year reduction in a price
why then did we learn in a משנה
a סלע coin and a פונדיון coin, the yearly price

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari said to Ravina:

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, שְׁבִיעִית לֹא תַּעֲלֶה לוֹ מִן הַגֵּירוּעַ!
phrases.english: If so, the Sabbatical Year should not count for him in the deduction!
phrases.notes: This is about redeeming a field given to הקדש. The price is figured year by year.

phrases.aramaic: אַלְּמָה תְּנַן: נוֹתֵן סֶלַע וּפוּנְדְּיוֹן לְשָׁנָה!
phrases.english: Why did we learn: he gives a sela and a pundeyon per year!
phrases.notes: That משנה is in ערכין. 'Per year' includes שביעית too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that שביעית is completely cancelled by the King
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If שביעית were completely cancelled, it would be left out of the yearly redemption price. The משנה counts it anyway.

steps.title: The field is still usable for spreading out produce
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that the redemption case is different. Even during שביעית, the field can be used to spread produce out to dry, so it still has value that year.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There it is different, because the field is fit for spreading out produce on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge. This ends this round of back-and-forth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Planting is forbidden in שביעית, but the land still has a use: spreading out produce to dry. The redemption price pays for the field's value, so that year still counts. For a sold field, שביעית does not count because it is cancelled by the King (Step 15), not because of a missing harvest.
steps.whatToRemember: A sold field counts 'years of produce in the world.' שביעית is left out of that count because it is cancelled by the King. Yet שביעית still counts toward the price of redeeming a field from הקדש, because the land is still usable for spreading out produce.

phrases.english: He said to him: There it is different,
since it is fit for spreading out produce on it.
phrases.notes: He means laying produce out on the field to dry. That is allowed even in שביעית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: the field keeps a usable value during שביעית
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If שביעית is cancelled, it should not count toward the redemption price.
steps.terutzMaskana: The redemption price reflects any use of the land, and spreading out produce is still possible in שביעית, so it counts.

steps.title: שמואל: No reduction if the tenant never planted
steps.stepSummary: שמואל limits the משנה's rule. A tenant may reduce his payment for a regional disaster only if he planted the field and then grasshoppers ate the crop. If he never planted at all, the owner can say his merit might have saved his field.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: The rule that a tenant may reduce his payment applies only when he planted the field, it sprouted, and grasshoppers ate it. But if he never planted it at all, he may not reduce. The owner can tell him: Had you planted it, the פסוק might have come true for me: "They will not be shamed in a time of evil, and in days of famine they will be satisfied."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. שמואל explains when a tenant may lower his payment because a disaster hit the whole region.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lets a tenant reduce his payment when a regional disaster like grasshoppers ruins the field. שמואל adds a condition: the tenant must actually have planted. If he never planted, the owner can argue that his own merit might have protected his field even during the disaster.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this rule when... (a way of limiting a rule)
Would have come true for me

steps.whatToRemember: According to שמואל, a tenant who never planted cannot blame a regional disaster. The owner can say that his own merit might have saved the field.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
They only taught this when he planted it
phrases.notes: This refers to the משנה's rule that a tenant may reduce his payment when a disaster hits the whole region.

phrases.english: and it sprouted and grasshoppers ate it.
But if he did not plant it at all – no,
because he can say to him: Had you planted it
there would have been fulfilled for me
"They will not be shamed in the time of evil
and in the days of famine they will be satisfied."
phrases.notes: תהלים 37:19

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: לֹא שָׁנוּ, אֶלָּא שֶׁזְּרָעָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the discussion of שביעית and the redemption of fields.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tenant may reduce his payment for a regional disaster only if he planted the field. If he never planted, the owner can claim his merit might have protected it.

steps.title: Challenge from the shepherd who left his flock
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת quotes a ברייתא. A shepherd who left his flock is liable only if he could have saved the animals. Nobody tells him that the owner's merit would have brought a miracle. This seems to go against שמואל's reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת objected: A shepherd left his flock and went to town. A wolf came and tore an animal, or a lion came and trampled one. We do not simply say that had he been there he would have saved them. Rather, we estimate: if he could have saved them, he is liable; if not, he is exempt. But why? Let the owner say: Had you been there, the פסוק would have come true for me: "Both the lion and the bear your servant struck!"
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת attacks שמואל's idea using a ברייתא about a shepherd who walked away from the animals he was watching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל let the owner argue that his merit might have changed what happened. If that argument works, the owner of the flock should also be able to say that a miracle would have happened if the shepherd had stayed, like when דוד struck the lion and the bear. But the ברייתא only looks at what the shepherd could normally have done, so it seems to reject this kind of argument.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet raises an objection:
A shepherd who was herding
and he left his flock and came to the town,
and a wolf came and tore,
and a lion came and trampled –
we do not say: Had he been there
he would have rescued them,
rather we estimate concerning him:
if he could have rescued them – he is liable,
and if not – he is exempt.
But why? Let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The owner of the animals is talking to the shepherd.

phrases.english: If you had been there
there would have been fulfilled for me
"Both the lion and the bear
your servant struck!"
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:36

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning שמואל used in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's argument that the owner can claim his merit would have protected his field.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If an owner can claim that his merit would have changed the outcome, the owner of a flock should also be able to claim a miracle would have saved his animals. Yet the ברייתא ignores that claim.

steps.title: The owner was not worthy of a miracle
steps.stepSummary: The shepherd can answer: if you were worthy of a miracle, you would have gotten one even without me, like רבי חנינא בן דוסא, whose goats brought home bears on their horns.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the shepherd can say to him: If you were worthy of a miracle, a miracle would have happened for you, like it did for רבי חנינא בן דוסא, whose goats brought back bears on their horns.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב ששת's challenge by explaining what the shepherd can say back to the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saving animals from a lion or bear without being able to do it naturally would be a real miracle. The shepherd argues that someone worthy of such a miracle gets it even with no shepherd there, as happened to רבי חנינא בן דוסא. Since no miracle happened, the owner clearly was not worthy, so the shepherd's being away made no difference.

phrases.english: Because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Now it is the shepherd answering the owner.

phrases.english: If you were worthy
for a miracle to happen to you,
a miracle would have happened for you
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some have the word in square brackets. Both mean the miracle would have happened.

phrases.english: like Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa
whose goats brought bears on their horns.
phrases.notes: This story is told in תענית 25a.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's challenge from step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the cases: saving animals from a lion would need a big miracle, which comes without a shepherd for those who deserve it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner could claim that his merit would have worked through the shepherd, just as in שמואל's case.
steps.terutzMaskana: A great miracle does not depend on the shepherd being there, so his absence did not cause the loss.

steps.title: But what about a small miracle?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: let the owner say that even if he was not worthy of a big miracle, he might have been worthy of a small one. The question continues on the next part of the daf.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the owner say to him: Granted that I was not worthy of a big miracle, but of a small miracle...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. The sentence is cut off here and continues on the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 20 only showed that the owner was not worthy of a big miracle that happens all by itself. The owner can reply that a smaller miracle, one that works through the shepherd like with דוד, might still have happened. That would bring back שמואל's kind of argument.

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The owner is talking to the shepherd again.

phrases.english: Granted that for a big miracle
I was not worthy –
for a small miracle...

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנֵימָא לֵיהּ: נְהִי דִּלְנִיסָּא רַבָּה לָא הֲוָה חֲזֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the owner was not worthy of a miracle like רבי חנינא בן דוסא's.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Not being worthy of a big miracle does not rule out a small miracle that would have worked through the shepherd.
